# Outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus infection in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease

**Authors:** Justine P Enns; Jiaqi Wang; Bohang Jiang; Shruthi Srivatsan; Emily N Kowalski; Xiaosong Wang; Zachary K Williams; Grace Qian; Jennifer Hanberg; Colebrooke Johnson; Madison Negron; Katarina J Bade; Alene Saavedra; Kevin T Mueller; Kathleen MM Vanni; Camille N Kotton; Jeffrey A Sparks; Zachary S Wallace; Naomi J Patel

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | bHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | cDivision of Rheumatology, Allergy and Immunology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | dRheumatology & Allergy Clinical Epidemiology Research Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | eDivision of Rheumatology, Inflammation, and Immunity, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | fDivision of Infectious Diseases, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common respiratory viral illness which can cause severe outcomes in older and immunosuppressed populations. There is little data regarding RSV outcomes among people with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs).

This retrospective cohort study examined risk factors for hospitalization in individuals with SARDs and documented RSV infection between 2015 and 2023 at Mass General Brigham (Boston, MA). Clinical data were collected from electronic health records. Multivariable adjusted logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with hospitalization for RSV infection.

Of 188 individuals with SARDs and RSV (mean age 68.5 years, 75.5% female), 96 (51.0%) were hospitalized. Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (aOR 1.16 per point, 95% CI: 1.04–1.31), Claims-Based Frailty Index (aOR 4.80 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95% CI: 2.32–9.94), and concurrent infection (aOR 2.52 vs. RSV alone, 95% CI: 1.07–5.92) were associated with increased odds of hospitalization. CD20 inhibitor treatment (aOR 3.84 vs. csDMARD, 95% CI: 0.99–15.20) and older age (OR 1.03 per year, 95% CI: 1.01–1.05) were associated with numerically increased odds of RSV hospitalization. Among hospitalized individuals, 56% required oxygen. There were 12 deaths within 90 days (12.5% of those hospitalized; 6% of all with RSV).

This study highlights the increased risk of severe outcomes of RSV infection in individuals with SARDs. Factors associated with RSV hospitalization included frailty, higher comorbidity burden, and concurrent infection at the time of RSV. These findings should inform clinical decisions regarding RSV vaccination and prevention strategies.

Keywords: Frailty, RSV, COVID19, Hospitalization, Autoimmune disease

## Introduction

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common viral infection that usually affects the upper respiratory tract. While RSV infection most often causes mild illness in the general adult population, it can cause severe respiratory illness, particularly in elderly and high-risk adults [1]. Data from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) between 2016 and 2023 estimates rates of RSV-associated hospitalization in the United States between 48.9 to 76.2 per 100,000 adults per season [2]. RSV-associated hospitalizations are overall less common than hospitalizations due to COVID-19 or influenza. However, prior to the availability of RSV vaccines in 2023, people with RSV experienced similar severe infection outcomes compared to those with COVID-19 or influenza among those not vaccinated for these viruses, and RSV outcomes were more severe than COVID-19 or influenza among vaccinated individuals [3]. Increased risk of worse RSV outcomes including hospitalization and mortality have been noted in individuals with a history of hematologic malignancies [4], hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [4,5], and solid organ transplantation [6,7]. Our understanding of other factors impacting RSV-related complications and death, however, particularly among individuals with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) remains limited.

This is of particular concern as individuals with SARDs may be at increased risk of severe infection due to the intrinsic pathobiology of the systemic disease as well as use of immunosuppressive treatment [8]. Thus, current guidelines for individuals with SARDs recommend routine vaccinations for vaccine-preventable respiratory diseases including influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal pneumonia, and others; the most recent American College of Rheumatology SARD vaccination guideline was published in 2022, prior to the approval of the RSV vaccine in the United States [13].

The approval of the first RSV vaccine in 2023 further emphasizes the need to understand risk factors for severe RSV infection to determine which populations would most benefit from vaccination. Three different RSV vaccines (Arexvy from GlaxoSmithKline [14], Abrysvo from Pfizer [15], and mRESVIA from Moderna [16]) are currently available in the US, and the CDC’s current recommendation is for RSV vaccination for all adults aged 75 years and older and for those aged 50–74 who are at increased risk of severe RSV [17].

There is currently little data regarding RSV outcomes among those with SARDs, particularly in relation to the associations of different disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). The objective of this study was to evaluate the risk of severe outcomes of RSV infections in individuals with SARDs and to identify risk factors for hospitalization during RSV infections within this population. We performed this study in the period prior to widespread availability of RSV vaccination.

## Methods

### Study design, participants, and exposures

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating factors associated with hospitalization during RSV infection among individuals with SARDs in a large healthcare system. Mass General Brigham (MGB) is a multi-center healthcare system that includes a total of 14 hospitals, including two tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), as well as other primary care and specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts, US area. We initially identified individuals who had both a positive laboratory test (either Polymerase Chain Reaction or antigen testing) for RSV in the outpatient setting, emergency department, or inpatient setting at MGB between June 1, 2015, and November 30, 2023, and any ICD-10 code for any SARD. Then, we performed manual electronic health record (EHR) review to confirm SARD diagnoses as well as the specific SARD type. The index date was the first RSV positive laboratory test among each patient with a prevalent SARD. This study was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board (2020P000833).

### Outcomes assessment

We performed a manual review of each individual’s EHR to ascertain clinical outcomes including RSV symptoms, hospitalization status, medical interventions, and death. RSV hospitalization was defined as admission to a hospital within 10 days of a positive RSV test and mortality was defined as death within 90 days of positive RSV test. Concurrent bacterial pneumonia was defined as confirmed and/or suspected pneumonia, based on at least any one of: 1) radiographic infiltrate consistent with pneumonia, 2) microbiological (e.g., sputum sample, bronchoalveolar lavage) evidence, and/or 3) treatment with antibiotics. Cause of death was obtained from review of the EHR (e.g., death certificate, relevant notes).

### Covariates of interest

We used electronic query to extract variables including demographics (e.g., age at index date of RSV infection, sex, race, ethnicity, Claims-Based Frailty Index [CFI], Charlson Comorbidity Index [CCI]) and clinical values (e.g., body mass index [BMI], estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] and hemoglobin A1c [Hgb A1c]). The CFI is a validated claims-based index which categorizes frailty on a deficit-accumulation model, categorizing individuals as robust (CFI <0.15), prefrail (0.15–0.24), or frail (>0.25) [18]. The CCI is a summary measure that incorporates a variety of different potential comorbidities and predicts 10-year survival [19]. We manually reviewed the EHR to collect other exposures of interest (e.g., SARD diagnosis and treatment, individual comorbidities, and concurrent infections). For analyses involving DMARD treatment, individuals were categorized into the following mutually exclusive hierarchical groups: no DMARD, conventional synthetic DMARD (csDMARD), targeted synthetic DMARD, TNF inhibitor, CD20 inhibitor, or other biologic DMARD (bDMARD), with the biologic taking precedence in those on multiple medications.

### Statistical analysis

We evaluated the association of baseline factors, including demographics, SARD diagnosis and treatment, comorbidities, frailty, and concurrent infections, with hospitalization during RSV infection. We used unadjusted and multivariable logistic regression to assess the association of these baseline factors with the odds of hospitalization during RSV infection. Multivariable analyses were adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, CCI, and CFI. To assess the robustness of our results, we performed a subgroup analysis in which we limited the population to those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or other forms of inflammatory arthritis. We also performed a secondary analysis with an outcome of hospitalization due to RSV infection. The level of significance was set as a two-tailed p < 0.05, and statistical analyses were conducted using SAS statistical software (version 9.4; SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC).

## Results

### Characteristics of the study population

Of 371 individuals with a positive RSV test result and any ICD-10 code for a SARD, 188 were included after confirmation of both prevalent SARD diagnosis and RSV infection. None had been vaccinated against RSV prior to infection. Of the 188 individuals included, the median (IQR) age was 69 (59, 77) years (Table 1). Most were White (74 %) followed by Black (8 %) and Asian (4 %); 2 % were Hispanic. The most common SARD categories were rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthritis (52 %), followed by systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other connective tissue diseases (CTD) (19 %) and polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) and/or giant cell arteritis (GCA) (10 %). Among all individuals, 68 % were on a DMARD; 52 % were on csDMARDs, 2 % were on targeted synthetic DMARDs, 24 % were on biologic DMARDs, and 44 % were on oral glucocorticoids. Forty-two people (22 %) had a concurrent viral, bacterial, or fungal infection as defined by a positive microbiologic test, indicative imaging findings, and/or clinical diagnosis and treatment by the treating team.

### Factors associated with hospitalization during RSV infection

Among 188 people with a SARD and RSV infection, 96 (51 %) were hospitalized during their RSV infection (Table 1). The mean age of those hospitalized during RSV infection was 72 years compared with 66 years for non-hospitalized individuals (p < 0.01) (Table 1). Older age had significantly higher odds of RSV hospitalization in unadjusted analyses (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.03 per year, 95 % CI [1.01–1.05]), and numerically higher risk in multivariable analyses (multivariable adjusted odds ratio [aOR] of 1.02 per year, 95 % CI: 0.996–1.04). Higher CCI (aOR 1.16 per point, 95 % CI: 1.04–1.31), frailty by CFI (aOR 4.80 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95 % CI: 2.32–9.94), and concurrent infection (aOR 2.52 vs. RSV alone, 95 % CI: 1.07–5.92) were associated with increased odds of hospitalization (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 1). Of the immunosuppressive medications evaluated, treatment with a CD20 inhibitor in the 12 months prior to RSV infection was associated with numerically higher odds of hospitalization (aOR 3.84 vs. csDMARD use, 95 % CI: 0.99–15.20).

*Fig. 1.: Factors associated with hospitalization during RSV infection.CCI: Charlson Comorbidity Index; csDMARD, conventional synthetic DMARD.*Multivariable model was adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, CCI, and Claims-Based Frailty Index (CFI).*

While pre-existing interstitial lung disease was not significantly associated with increased odds of hospitalization (aOR 2.23 vs. no interstitial lung disease, 95 % CI: 0.76–6.50). Of all individuals with interstitial lung disease (ILD) (n = 23), 17 (74 %) were hospitalized during RSV infection; ILD was associated with numerically higher odds of hospitalization (aOR 2.23 vs. no ILD, 95 % CI: 0.76–6.50). People who were hospitalized during infection had a lower eGFR than those not hospitalized in the 6 months prior to RSV diagnosis: the median lowest eGFR was 74 ml/min/1.73m2 over the prior 6 months in those not hospitalized vs. 54 ml/min/1.73m2 in those hospitalized (p < 0.01) (Table 1) (aOR of 0.98 per 1-unit increase in ml/min/1.73m2, 95 % CI: 0.97–1.00, Supplementary Table 1).

In the secondary analysis with the outcome of hospitalization due to RSV infection, frailty remained significantly associated with hospitalization (aOR 3.97 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95 % CI: 1.98–7.95) (Supplementary Table 2). Concurrent infection (aOR 2.12 vs. no concurrent infection, 95 % CI: 0.96–4.67) and CCI (aOR 1.10 per unit, 95 % CI: 0.99–1.23) were numerically but not significantly associated with hospitalization, and age (aOR 1.04 per year, 95 % CI: 1.01–1.06) and interstitial lung disease (aOR 3.63 vs. no interstitial lung disease, 95 % CI: 1.27–10.34) were significantly associated with hospitalization in this analysis.

### RA and inflammatory arthritis subgroup analysis

A subgroup analysis was performed among individuals with RA or other inflammatory arthritis (n = 98) (Supplementary Tables 3–4). Similar to the overall cohort, frailty (aOR 5.15 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95 % CI: 1.78–14.87) was associated with significantly increased odds of hospitalization. In this cohort, age, concurrent bacterial pneumonia, and lower eGFR were numerically but not significantly associated with higher odds of hospitalization.

### In-hospital interventions and deaths for individuals with SARDs during RSV infection

Of the 96 individuals hospitalized during RSV infection, 84 % were for RSV or infection-related complications and 56 % required varying levels of oxygen support (Table 2). The greatest proportion of those requiring support required nasal cannula oxygen (40 %), and a minority required high-flow or non-invasive ventilation (including continuous or bilevel positive airway pressure) (8 %), invasive mechanical ventilation (7 %), or extracorporeal membrane support (ECMO) (1 %). Within 30 days of hospital discharge, 26 % of hospitalized individuals were readmitted. Of all individuals with RSV infection, 12 individuals (6 %) died within 90 days of RSV infection and 7 of these deaths (58 %) were attributed to RSV (Supplementary Table 5). The individuals who died within 90 days of RSV infection were older than those in the overall cohort (mean age of 79 years); three individuals were between ages 60 and 75 and the remaining nine were older than age 75. Half of those who died were receiving treatment with a csDMARD or bDMARD for their SARD; the other half were not using any DMARD. Eleven of the twelve (92 %) had pre-existing cardiovascular and/or pulmonary comorbidities at or prior to RSV infection, and 4 (33 %) had moderate to severe chronic kidney disease.

## Discussion

In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated clinical outcomes of individuals with SARDs and RSV infection within a large, multi-institutional healthcare system in the United States and identified factors associated with increased risk of being hospitalized during RSV infection. This is the first study to investigate the characteristics and outcomes of individuals with SARDs and RSV infection. We found that frailty, concurrent infection, and greater overall comorbidity burden were associated with increased odds of hospitalization during RSV infection and that higher eGFR was associated with lower odds of hospitalization. Older age and use of CD20 inhibitors were associated with numerically higher odds of hospitalization in multivariable analyses. For individuals who required hospitalization during RSV infection, over half required some level of oxygen report. Twelve individuals (6 % of those overall with infection and 12.5 % of those hospitalized) died within 90 days of infection of all causes, 7 of which were directly attributable to RSV infection. Of those who died, the average age was 10 years older than that of the overall cohort of those with SARDs and RSV infection, and most had cardiovascular and/or pulmonary comorbidities at the time of RSV infection. Thus, individuals with SARDs are at risk of poor RSV infection outcomes, supporting current recommendations for RSV vaccination in this vulnerable group.

Our finding of older age being associated with higher odds of hospitalization on univariable analysis and in multivariable analysis with the outcome of hospitalization due to RSV infection is consistent with prior studies investigating RSV in the adult population. Older age (>75 and >85 years) has been described in the general population as a factor for more severe RSV disease and RSV-related mortality [20,21]. Older adults have greater risk of complications from numerous infections including viral respiratory illnesses and bacterial pneumonias due to age-related changes in both innate and adaptive immune responses, creating an imbalance between chronic low-level inflammation and reduced adaptive immune efficacy to pathogenic targets [22,23]. We also found frailty, another age-associated factor but distinct from chronological age, to be significantly associated with increased odds of hospitalization both during and due to RSV infection. Age was not associated with significantly higher odds of hospitalization in multi-variable analyses, though our multivariable analysis was adjusted for CFI, among other factors. Autoimmune disease is a risk factor for the onset of frailty and frailty itself is a risk factor for adverse outcomes for individuals with rheumatologic disease [24]. Frailty has been independently associated with serious outcomes and mortality in other SARDs, including rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis [25,26].

Greater comorbidity burden was another factor that was associated with increased odds of hospitalization, with this study demonstrating that those hospitalized had lower eGFRs and higher CCI score (reflecting total burden of comorbidity) than those not hospitalized. Of the 12 individuals who died within 90 days of RSV infection, 11 had substantial pre-existing cardiopulmonary morbidities including heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), ILD, asthma, and pulmonary malignancy, reflecting the impact that non-SARD diagnoses have in contributing to adverse outcomes from RSV infection. The impact of pre-existing diseases on worse RSV outcomes has also been seen in other studies of the general population, with cardiorespiratory disease and obesity identified as risk factors for ICU admission among individuals hospitalized for RSV. Pre-existing pulmonary (e.g., from underlying COPD, ILD, asthma) and cardiac disease were identified as risk factors for intubation [21,27]. This has particular relevance to those with SARDs as these individuals are at increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease compared to the general population [28] and many SARDs can cause renal involvement and subsequent progressive renal damage [29]. ILD can be a significant complication in a wide range of SARDs, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, and myositis, with a wide range in prevalence estimates between countries and healthcare settings [30]. In this study, there were significantly more individuals with ILD who were hospitalized but this significance was lost in the multivariable analysis, likely related to sample size (only 23 with ILD).

The impact of immunosuppressive medications on increased risk of severe infection due to RSV remains an area of active investigation. A prior study looking broadly at immunocompromised people with RSV found that those treated with chronic immunosuppressive medications were more likely to require hospitalization but only included 20 total adult participants being treated and did not differentiate between different categories of immunosuppressive medications [31]. Additionally, immunocompromised individuals have been shown to have a heterogenous and often reduced antibody response to the new RSV vaccine, with up to 40 % of participants having inadequate antibody responses at 4 weeks post-vaccination, substantially lower than that reported in the immunocompetent population [32,33]. We found that treatment with CD20 inhibitors was associated with numerically increased odds of hospitalization (aOR 3.84, 95 % CI: 0.99–15.20) but did not find significant associations between glucocorticoids (either low-dose or higher doses) or TNF inhibitors and hospitalization. The confidence interval for TNF inhibitors was quite wide, and the numerically increased odds in those not receiving DMARDs may be due to confounding by indication, with individuals who are older, frailer, or have higher comorbidity burden—all factors associated with increased risk of hospitalization—being unable to tolerate or having contraindications to DMARDs. Some individuals in this group may be receiving glucocorticoid monotherapy, possibly at higher doses given the lack of steroid-sparing DMARD, which may also increase risk. CD20 inhibitors have been shown to significantly increase the risk of serious infections, including viral respiratory infections and lower respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia; however, older age and longer duration of underlying SARD among those treated with CD20 inhibitors may also partially explain the results [34,35]. In those with inflammatory bowel disease, systemic glucocorticoids were associated with increased risk of hospitalization [36].

Research in other respiratory viruses has evaluated both vaccine safety as well as outcomes and relationship to viremia. Risks of severe outcomes in individuals with influenza and COVID-19 infections are higher in those with SARDs than in those in the general population [9–11]. Reassuringly, studies on COVID-19 vaccination have demonstrated a reassuring safety profile in the SARD patient population, including in those on DMARDs. Despite possible impaired responses, most individuals generally achieve adequate humoral responses to vaccination as well as evidence of clinical efficacy with decreased rates of hospitalization following vaccination [12]. Studies on other viral infections such as COVID-19 have also found a correlation between the presence and duration of RSV viremia with severe outcomes [37–39]. While this retrospective study did not evaluate RSV viral levels, the relationship between inability to clear the virus due to either the SARD or its treatment and severe outcomes including hospitalization should be an area of future investigation.

Of the 188 SARD individuals with positive RSV tests included in this study, 54 % were hospitalized. This percentage is notably higher than those in other population-level and disease-specific studies of RSV. Studies of adults who initially tested positive for RSV in the outpatient setting estimate that between 5–7 % of individuals overall or 7–9 % of “higher risk” individuals (defined as those ≥65 years or those with asthma, COPD, or congestive heart failure) were hospitalized within 30 days of testing [40,41]. Reasons for the discrepancy between the higher rate of hospitalization in this study compared to others may relate to ascertainment bias, as we identified people with confirmed positive tests within our healthcare system or may relate to additional risks in the setting of SARD diagnoses and immunosuppression. The results of this study on individuals with SARDs are comparable to a similar study which looked at outcomes of people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) with RSV infection, where 45.4 % of those with IBD required hospitalization [36].

Our study has several strengths. First, we systematically identified individuals with SARDs from the entire MGB EHR and manually confirmed all diagnoses. Second, we identified test-confirmed RSV infections using data from the EHR. Third, details regarding comorbidities and medications—particularly immunomodulatory and immunosuppressive medications—prescribed at the time of RSV infection were available. Fourth, we manually reviewed all cases and were able to ascertain detailed information regarding hospitalization, if pertinent, relation to RSV, and causes of death.

Our study also has several limitations. First, we only captured individuals who tested positive for RSV and thus did not identify individuals with either asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic RSV infection who were not tested or who did not present to clinical attention. As RSV testing outside of a healthcare facility is limited and home tests are uncommon, our denominator of individuals with RSV infection is certainly an underestimate, and the absolute proportion with hospitalization and/or death represent overestimates. This is further supported by the fact that our study only had 5 total patients who were classified as robust by the CFI, all of whom were not hospitalized, supportive of this study capturing an overall more frail population that was more likely to have significantly symptomatic or severe RSV infection leading to testing. Second, we did not collect detailed information about rheumatic disease activity or SARD medication interruption around the time of RSV infection which could have potentially impacted results. Third, sample size limited the number of people captured in the different DMARD treatment categories and in those receiving higher doses of glucocorticoids, likely limiting our study’s ability to detect statistical significance. Fourth, the population only includes people with SARDs and thus does not allow for any comparison of outcomes between those with SARDs and the general population. Fifth, while we assessed the first RSV infection for each individual within our study period, we did not have data on RSV infection prior to the study period and thus were not able to assess differences in outcomes between those with a first versus second RSV infection. Sixth, we were not able to assess whether underlying cardiovascular disease (present in 23.9 % of our study population at baseline) was exacerbated following RSV infection. Finally, in defining presence of a concurrent bacterial or fungal pneumonia, we used a broad definition including radiographic or microbiological evidence of disease as well as the treating team’s clinical diagnosis, which risks over-estimating the prevalence of concurrent infection.

## Conclusions

Clinicians who take care of people with SARDs should consider these findings when discussing and recommending age-appropriate RSV vaccination with their patients and when reviewing related prevention strategies such as pneumococcal, COVID-19, and influenza vaccinations, particularly as concurrent infections were associated with increased odds of requiring hospitalization in the setting of RSV infection.
